Abhinav Kumar $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Vishal Purohit $\textcircled{1}$ , Vandana Bharti $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Rishav Singh, Member, IEEE, and Sanjay Kumar Singh $\textcircled{1}$ , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—Deep learning demonstrates its efficacy and potential to solve challenging computer vision problems in medical and other industrial applications. Federated learning is a learning paradigm that facilitates collaborative learning in a federation of users without exchanging actual data with a single authority like a server. However, federated learning provides only a basic level of privacy and robustness and is vulnerable to model poisoning and model inversion attacks in hostile training environments. Hence, in this article, we propose MediSecFed—a secure framework for federated learning in a hostile environment. Compared to the widely used FedAvg, our method relies on simple and practical ideas from knowledge distillation and model inversion to ensure additional security and privacy features. Our approach achieves knowledge exchange among participating entities without sharing model parameters as FedAvg does, thus protecting the privacy of the local data from the server and significantly reducing communication costs. We evaluate our method on two chest $\pmb { \mathrm { x } }$ -ray datasets. Our method outperforms FedAvg by $15 \%$ on both datasets in a hostile environment. Our method will also continue to maintain good performance even if the number of malicious participating entities increases. Robustness to learn in a malicious environment while preserving privacy with reduced communication costs makes our method more desirable and efficient than that of FedAvg.
Index Terms—COVID-19, data-free knowledge distillation, federated learning (FL), medical data security, privacypreserving.
I. INTRODUCTION

W ITH the unprecedented growth of computer softwareand hardware technologies, an increasing amount of medical data from medical institutions, patients, health insurers, and pharma industries are becoming readily accessible. This access affords enormous scope for data science technologies to extract data-driven insights and improve the quality of medical predictions. The deep learning industry has seen significant growth in the last several years, and it has tremendous scope in building useful and high potential IoT-based applications. With AlexNet’s breakthrough in the ImageNet competition in 2012, more advanced deep neural networks (ResNet, VGGNet, and several others) have been developed. Deep learning is now widely used in industrial applications by utilizing vast amounts of generated datasets. Recently, the deep learning model has shown its potential in healthcare applications as a feature extractor for cancer prediction [1].

However, to produce good results, these networks require a huge amount of computation and a vast number of datasets. As a result, the full potential of these networks can only be realized through extensive computational programming with large datasets. In the distributed setting of healthcare applications, medical data are typically fragmented and private, making it difficult to create robust results among communities. Different medical institutions may be able to access only the clinical records of their respective patient communities. However, these records are susceptible since they contain patients’ private health information. Strict regulations and government laws have been devised to manage the process of obtaining and analyzing such data. This presents a major hurdle for creating successful, generalized, deep learning-based models that require varied and large amounts of medical data. Data sharing among medical institutions is becoming increasingly desirable to minimize the shortage and distribution biases of medical data and enhance model performance on critical tasks.

Moreover, sharing medical data with a third party is a major concern to the data owner or institution, even if the third party is well known or anonymous. Besides that, due to the potential conflict of interest in each medical institution, it is also impractical to aggregate sensitive data from IoT devices in different hospitals to build an efficient model for healthcare diagnostic systems.

content_list.text: Therefore, federated learning (FL) [2] has recently emerged as a promising solution for this problem in a distributed environment. The overview of the classical FL scheme is presented in Fig. 1. It enables training a shared global model using a central server while retaining all sensitive data in the local medical institution where it belongs. FL has tremendous potential for connecting fragmented healthcare data sources while maintaining privacy. It enables learning from distributed data sources by aggregating the locally obtained model parameters without transmitting sensitive health data. However, there are major impediments to the scalable deployment of secure and truly privacy-preserving FL for sensitive applications. Existing FL algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial updates [3] and backdoor attacks [4], and they can expose sensitive information on local datasets [5]. This jeopardizes personal privacy and has the potential to result in unforeseen economic and life losses. In some ways, the privacy issues in FL constitute a significant impediment to the marketing and development of industrial artificial intelligence based applications.

The key challenges in federated training are communication overheads and client heterogeneity: Training data, as well as hardware and computing resources, can vary dramatically between clients, e.g., when training on mobile devices. The primary goal of the medical data classification problem is to train a model that can produce good results on the test datasets. To accomplish this, we train a huge model, which could be an ensemble of several individual trained models or just a very large model trained using a regularizer such as a Dropout. Once the huge model (teacher) is trained, we utilize a process known as distillation to transfer the complicated knowledge gained by the huge model to a smaller model (student) that is more suited for deployment in devices with limited memory and compute power. The huge model must generalize properly so that when we are distilling knowledge to the smaller model, it can generalize in the same way as the large model. Hence, knowledge distillation (KD) [6], a new technique for compacting and accelerating neural networks, is developed to maintain comparable performance while keeping the constraints in mind.

Despite the favorable outcomes, KD techniques rely heavily on huge amounts of training data to transmit information from pretrained teacher models to students. However, owing to privacy or transmission concerns, the training data are sometimes not shared alongside the pretrained models, rendering these approaches inapplicable. Another limitation is KD’s reliance on proxy data, as the selection of proxy data, which requires careful consideration, is a critical factor in distillation performance. To solve this issue, data-free KD is proposed [7]. Data-free KD generally uses the generated surrogate data based on the large network (teacher) for training a fast and compact (student) network. Some researchers [7] prefer to generate surrogate data by using the statistical metadata of the activation in a large network (teacher).

While model inversion (MI) [8] is another strategy for generating synthesized data for training student networks, it is a critical step in the data-free KD process, with the objective of recovering training data from pretrained teacher models. Student models may be easily learned using the generated synthetic data by directly using the data-driven KD methods. Recently, a generative adversarial network has demonstrated its potential in image synthesis and translation, becoming a popular choice for such applications [9]. In general, sensitive and confidential data in the healthcare domain necessitates security in a distributed environment. In order to be processed through deep learning based approaches, data must be centralized, but owing to medical data privacy regulations, collecting and sharing patients’ data in a centralized data server is often not feasible. Also, in the case of a new disease such as COVID-19, there is a lack of vast amounts of annotated training data at a single site. Therefore, in this study, we have attempted to tackle the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms.

Motivation and Contribution: FL ensures a basic level of privacy by not exchanging the actual data with any other participating entity. Yet it trades the model’s parameters with a server. To subvert the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms, we propose a method called MediSecFed. Our approach takes inspiration from KD and model inversion literature to build a framework that ensures good performance without trading off client privacy. Inherently, our method reduces the communication cost significantly while preserving privacy. To the best of our knowledge, most of the works [10]–[13] tackle this issue for natural images, but their use on computer vision tasks on medical images is unknown. Some of the assumptions made in the works [10] and [11] are unfair to the medical domain due to strict regulations, compliance rules, and the lack of availability of large, labeled datasets. Our experimentation on the two medical datasets—-COVIDx-8B [14] and COVIDx-8A [14]—-reveals that our method has better performance than FedAvg [15] in malicious environments. Our objective is to showcase a possible research direction for training a deep learning model for medical application in a secure and privacy-preserved manner. The main contributions of our article can be summarized as follows.

1) The proposed MediSecFed uses the model inversion technique to obtain the dataset for effective KD in a collaborative environment. Unlike others, we do not rely on publicly available labeled or unlabeled medical data for
KD since it is expensive to gather and annotate data in the medical domain.

2) MediSecFed shows a significant ability to learn in an environment when $20 \%$ and $40 \%$ of total participating clients are malicious clients and outperforms methods such as FedAvg by $15 \%$ on two medical datasets. Our method performs well on data gathered from multiple medical X-ray scanners and data originating from different geographical locations.

3) Our method eliminates the need to share model parameters with a single entity such as a server and secures the learned model locally. Additionally, our method is less affected by noisy malicious participants, unlike FedAvg, which does not show any signs of learning. Our method does not allow the server to perform model inversion attacks since the model parameters are never shared.

4) By allowing participants to choose desired architectures based on their compute capability and tasks, MediSecFed does not restrict the hypothesis search space. Also, MediSecFed is modular, as one can add other security and privacy features such as robust aggregation and differential privacy without significant modifications.

5) Our method exchanges logits instead of the model parameters with the server, making our method communication significantly more efficient and practical in scenarios with slower connection speeds. Unlike FedAvg, our method does not compel all the clients to have the same model after the training process, as the global model does not exist in our method. Instead, each client learns a model tailored to its specific data distribution needs.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II provides the background description. In Section III, the proposed approach has been thoroughly elucidated. Experimental setup and result analysis on two medical data sets are presented in Section IV. Finally, Section V concludes this article.
II. PRELIMINARIES
In this section, we briefly introduced the terminologies which are closely related to our work.
A. Knowledge Distillation

KD is a compression scheme, also known as teacher–student compression, proposed by [16] that allows for the training of a smaller compact student network under the supervision of a larger pretrained teacher network or ensemble of networks, without the need for costly computation and storage. In the work [17], the authors formally introduced and generalized the term “KD,” which has since become popular among researchers. They tried to match the softmax activation function of the student’s logit with the softmax temperature activation function of the large network (teacher’s) logit. KD is widely used in knowledge transfer and model compression. However, when compared to other compression techniques, KD is capable of downsizing the network without regard for the structural difference between the teacher and student network model. Furthermore, ensemble distillation was also studied by the authors where ensemble of teacher models were considered, and where knowledge was distilled from the ensemble of network to student by doing an average of logit of the ensemble networks [18], [19]. Most of these approaches used real-world data for KD, but they could not handle cases where distillation data are not readily available. To overcome the real-world dataset dependency for KD, data-free KD was proposed in which synthetic data or metadata was used for KD [20]. DeepInversion [21] has been recently proposed in the same spirit.
B. Federated KD

The unavailability of large amounts of data, especially for the medical domain, due to data privacy concerns and legal constraints, while training a deep neural network in a distributed computation system is one of the challenging problems. FL can help to solve this problem to some extent. However, in the case of FL, model parameters are generally transferred in each communication round. Sharing a large number of parameters of deep networks incurs additional computation and communication costs. In medical domain, data collection and annotation are critical and costly tasks. Data annotation, particularly for medical images, necessitates significant effort as well as domain expertise. Federated KD [22] is thus proposed to address the aforementioned issues as well as user heterogeneity. It uses unlabeled data labeled by the teacher model (T) to transfer information from the teacher model to the small or compact student model (S). It has the potential to lessen dependency on labeled data while also ensuring privacy and security. The goal of federated KD is to reduce the L2 loss between the output logits of the teacher model (T) and the output logits of the student (S). C. Model Inversion

Model inversion (MI) is an important step in data-free KD. It came to light when researchers were thinking about security concerns. They attempted to discover whether there could be an approach to recover training samples from a pretrained model. It has been studied for various purposes over the years. The main goal of MI is to reconstruct input samples from the parameters of a previously trained model. It was first proposed by the authors in [25] to improve understanding of deep representation of a neural network. Recently, MI paradigms have shown their efficacy in knowledge transfer that lead to data-free KD [7], [21].

C. Model Inversion

Recently, model inversion techniques have shown great promise for reverse-engineering the frozen model to generate the dataset on which the frozen model was trained. As mentioned in Section III-B, the features of medical images differ significantly compared to natural images, and even among the medical images, the features vary a lot. For example, the features of histopathology data are different from chest X-rays. Some of the works [10], [11] on natural images assume a public dataset is made available to clients, and KD is done using a public dataset. However, there are hardly any medical datasets of the same scale as ImageNet in the medical domain. Hence, it is not practical to assume a publicly available medical dataset for KD. Thus, our method relies on generating images from a frozen model trained on a dataset that belongs to a similar manifold. We use DeepInversion [21] to generate the images. The model inversion process starts with a random matrix of similar size as the images to be generated. DeepInversion optimizes the input while regularizing the distribution of intermediate feature maps using information stored in the batch normalization layers of the frozen model. Since batch norm layers are crucial for DeepInversion to work, it is necessary to know the architecture of the pretrained model, which we believe is a fair assumption since knowing the model architecture does not leak any privacy.
D. Model Security and Communication Efficiency

1) Model Security and Poisoning: This section details some of the security features enjoyed by our method over other algorithms like FedAvg. FedAvg enables multiple data holders to train a global model without sharing their data but by sharing their training gradients/parameters [27], [28]. Algorithms like FedAvg are not robust to attacks like poisoning via label flip poisoning or the addition of random noise. Even a single malicious client can alter the global model. Since a deep learning model can remember the training data, exchanging the model parameters with a malicious server violates the desired level of privacy. Hence, directly exchanging the model parameter/gradients is not a great idea, especially in the medical domain. On the contrary, MediSecFed significantly reduces the updates from the model parameters’ size to its output dimension. As per the work carried out in [11], a reduction in the size of the updates significantly boosts the robustness guarantee when robust aggregation algorithms are used. Furthermore, since MediSecFed does not share the model parameters with the server, the probability of model inversion attacks is close to zero. Also, unlike FedAvg, MediSecFed does not produce a single global model. Instead, each client will have the model tailored for its local dataset with some knowledge shared by the other participants via the KD process. Finally, the experimental results presented in Section IV reveal that MediSecFed is relatively robust to poisoning attacks like random noise addition. All these security and privacy features offered by our method provide a considerable advantage for a system deployed in the real world where adversaries try to hamper the overall performance of the training process.

2) Communication Efficiency: Apart from solid security features, our method is communication efficient compared to established methods like FedAvg. Consider a simple training environment with all clients with the same neural network architecture as ResNet-18. There is a total of 11 million trainable parameters in

ResNet-18. In FedAvg, the trainable parameters are exchanged in every communication round. Considering the parameters use floating-point 32 precision, the total size of weights is $4 4 ~ \mathrm { M B }$ which has to be uploaded by the client in every communication round. FedAvg is more demanding for clients with weak network connections, and the possibility of failing to upload is high because of the enormous size of the weights. It is highly likely to have an asymmetric network where upload speed is slower than download speeds in real-world applications. In MediSecFed, in every communication round, we send the logits corresponding to the number of classes in the output layer, which is very low, mostly in kilobytes (KBs). Our method improves communication efficiency by reducing the number of parameters shared from 11 million to just 10 (if the output layer of the neural network has ten classes).
We believe the above security features and communication efficiency of our method can open up industrial use cases that were not possible before with FedAvg.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS

In this section, we first provide details about the datasets used in our experiments, the details about CNN architecture and hyperparameters values are provided in Section IV-B, followed by the evaluation of the effectiveness of proposed MediSecFed in Section IV-C.
A. Datasets and Data Distribution

We evaluate the model performance on two medical datasets: modified COVIDX-8B [14] and COVIDX-8A [14]. The modified COVIDX-8B dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8B, and it consists of 5322 Chest X-Ray images of various heights and width, out of which 4922 are training images, and 400 are test images pertaining to two classes— Covid and non-Covid. The modified COVIDX-8 A dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8 A, and it has 5585 training images of various dimensions and has 400 test images pertaining to three classes—normal, pneumonia, and Covid. Both the datasets are sourced from multiple publicly available repositories, making our dataset heterogeneous. We have ensured that both datasets contain almost equal samples for all the classes by undersampling from parent datasets. Both datasets are challenging because the X-rays are captured by different devices and sourced from different geographical locations. To generate the synthetic data used for KD, we use the publicly available frozen model DenseNet-121 [29] trained on CheXpert for chest X-ray image generation.
B. Implementation Details and Hyperparameter Tuning

Our training framework relies on FedML [30], which is an open-source FL library. The total number of clients involved in the experiments is varied from five to fifteen, and all clients are available in each communication round. We use ResNet18 architecture for our homogeneous architecture experiments, and for heterogeneous client architectures, we use ResNet18 and ResNet34. We split the training dataset into train and validation sets. Validation set is used for hyperparameter tuning. We use augmentation strategies like random cropping and random rotation for X-rays (both datasets). We use the RayTune package available in the PyTorch framework to find the best set of hyperparameters. Finally, we fix the same hyperparameters, image size, architecture, and augmentation strategies for a fair comparison across all the experiments. As the designed set of experiments are computationally demanding, we crop the input to $1 2 8 \times 1 2 8$ and use Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0005. We use batch size 16 and run each experiment for at least 200 communication rounds in the case of distributed learning methods or 200 epochs in the case of local training settings. All the experiments were carried out on NVIDIA A100 GPU.

As the data is distributed across multiple clients, it is difficult for any DL model to achieve very high accuracy. Apart from the imbalance dataset and a small number of samples per class, the images in these datasets are sourced from different scanning machines from varied geographical locations. These characteristics of the dataset make the problem even harder. Hence, the results presented in Table I may not be the best or state of the art. V. CONCLUSION

In this article, we have designed a new method called MediSecFed, which has leveraged the combination of techniques from KD and model inversion to perform learning in a collaborative training environment with no risk of exposing the local model or the data to a server or a third party. Furthermore, our extensive analysis of two chest $\mathbf { X }$ -ray datasets revealed the efficacy of our method, especially in a noisy environment, and outperformed FedAvg by $15 \%$ . Our method was communication efficient, and hence it can be used with slower connection speeds. We have used unbalanced non-i.i.d. data to evaluate the model’s performance, making our method suitable for any real-world industrial application.

In the future, we would like to extend our work to further improve the accuracy of our method by enhancing the diversity of the generated data used for KD. Also, we would like to explore the use of our method on other medical datasets.

MediSecFed: Private and Secure Medical Image Classification in the Presence of Malicious Clients

Abhinav Kumar $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Vishal Purohit $\textcircled{1}$ , Vandana Bharti $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Rishav Singh, Member, IEEE, and Sanjay Kumar Singh $\textcircled{1}$ , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—Deep learning demonstrates its efficacy and potential to solve challenging computer vision problems in medical and other industrial applications. Federated learning is a learning paradigm that facilitates collaborative learning in a federation of users without exchanging actual data with a single authority like a server. However, federated learning provides only a basic level of privacy and robustness and is vulnerable to model poisoning and model inversion attacks in hostile training environments. Hence, in this article, we propose MediSecFed—a secure framework for federated learning in a hostile environment. Compared to the widely used FedAvg, our method relies on simple and practical ideas from knowledge distillation and model inversion to ensure additional security and privacy features. Our approach achieves knowledge exchange among participating entities without sharing model parameters as FedAvg does, thus protecting the privacy of the local data from the server and significantly reducing communication costs. We evaluate our method on two chest $\pmb { \chi }$ -ray datasets. Our method outperforms FedAvg by $15 \%$ on both datasets in a hostile environment. Our method will also continue to maintain good performance even if the number of malicious participating entities increases. Robustness to learn in a malicious environment while preserving privacy with reduced communication costs makes our method more desirable and efficient than that of FedAvg.
Index Terms—COVID-19, data-free knowledge distillation, federated learning (FL), medical data security, privacypreserving.
I. INTRODUCTION

W ITH the unprecedented growth of computer softwareand hardware technologies, an increasing amount of medical data from medical institutions, patients, health insurers, and pharma industries are becoming readily accessible. This access affords enormous scope for data science technologies to extract data-driven insights and improve the quality of medical predictions. The deep learning industry has seen significant growth in the last several years, and it has tremendous scope in building useful and high potential IoT-based applications. With AlexNet’s breakthrough in the ImageNet competition in 2012, more advanced deep neural networks (ResNet, VGGNet, and several others) have been developed. Deep learning is now widely used in industrial applications by utilizing vast amounts of generated datasets. Recently, the deep learning model has shown its potential in healthcare applications as a feature extractor for cancer prediction [1].

However, to produce good results, these networks require a huge amount of computation and a vast number of datasets. As a result, the full potential of these networks can only be realized through extensive computational programming with large datasets. In the distributed setting of healthcare applications, medical data are typically fragmented and private, making it difficult to create robust results among communities. Different medical institutions may be able to access only the clinical records of their respective patient communities. However, these records are susceptible since they contain patients’ private health information. Strict regulations and government laws have been devised to manage the process of obtaining and analyzing such data. This presents a major hurdle for creating successful, generalized, deep learning-based models that require varied and large amounts of medical data. Data sharing among medical institutions is becoming increasingly desirable to minimize the shortage and distribution biases of medical data and enhance model performance on critical tasks.

Moreover, sharing medical data with a third party is a major concern to the data owner or institution, even if the third party is well known or anonymous. Besides that, due to the potential conflict of interest in each medical institution, it is also impractical to aggregate sensitive data from IoT devices in different hospitals to build an efficient model for healthcare diagnostic systems.

content_list.text: Therefore, federated learning (FL) [2] has recently emerged as a promising solution for this problem in a distributed environment. The overview of the classical FL scheme is presented in Fig. 1. It enables training a shared global model using a central server while retaining all sensitive data in the local medical institution where it belongs. FL has tremendous potential for connecting fragmented healthcare data sources while maintaining privacy. It enables learning from distributed data sources by aggregating the locally obtained model parameters without transmitting sensitive health data. However, there are major impediments to the scalable deployment of secure and truly privacy-preserving FL for sensitive applications. Existing FL algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial updates [3] and backdoor attacks [4], and they can expose sensitive information on local datasets [5]. This jeopardizes personal privacy and has the potential to result in unforeseen economic and life losses. In some ways, the privacy issues in FL constitute a significant impediment to the marketing and development of industrial artificial intelligence based applications.

The key challenges in federated training are communication overheads and client heterogeneity: Training data, as well as hardware and computing resources, can vary dramatically between clients, e.g., when training on mobile devices. The primary goal of the medical data classification problem is to train a model that can produce good results on the test datasets. To accomplish this, we train a huge model, which could be an ensemble of several individual trained models or just a very large model trained using a regularizer such as a Dropout. Once the huge model (teacher) is trained, we utilize a process known as distillation to transfer the complicated knowledge gained by the huge model to a smaller model (student) that is more suited for deployment in devices with limited memory and compute power. The huge model must generalize properly so that when we are distilling knowledge to the smaller model, it can generalize in the same way as the large model. Hence, knowledge distillation (KD) [6], a new technique for compacting and accelerating neural networks, is developed to maintain comparable performance while keeping the constraints in mind.

Despite the favorable outcomes, KD techniques rely heavily on huge amounts of training data to transmit information from pretrained teacher models to students. However, owing to privacy or transmission concerns, the training data are sometimes not shared alongside the pretrained models, rendering these approaches inapplicable. Another limitation is KD’s reliance on proxy data, as the selection of proxy data, which requires careful consideration, is a critical factor in distillation performance. To solve this issue, data-free KD is proposed [7]. Data-free KD generally uses the generated surrogate data based on the large network (teacher) for training a fast and compact (student) network. Some researchers [7] prefer to generate surrogate data by using the statistical metadata of the activation in a large network (teacher).

While model inversion (MI) [8] is another strategy for generating synthesized data for training student networks, it is a critical step in the data-free KD process, with the objective of recovering training data from pretrained teacher models. Student models may be easily learned using the generated synthetic data by directly using the data-driven KD methods. Recently, a generative adversarial network has demonstrated its potential in image synthesis and translation, becoming a popular choice for such applications [9]. In general, sensitive and confidential data in the healthcare domain necessitates security in a distributed environment. In order to be processed through deep learning based approaches, data must be centralized, but owing to medical data privacy regulations, collecting and sharing patients’ data in a centralized data server is often not feasible. Also, in the case of a new disease such as COVID-19, there is a lack of vast amounts of annotated training data at a single site. Therefore, in this study, we have attempted to tackle the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms.

Motivation and Contribution: FL ensures a basic level of privacy by not exchanging the actual data with any other participating entity. Yet it trades the model’s parameters with a server. To subvert the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms, we propose a method called MediSecFed. Our approach takes inspiration from KD and model inversion literature to build a framework that ensures good performance without trading off client privacy. Inherently, our method reduces the communication cost significantly while preserving privacy. To the best of our knowledge, most of the works [10]–[13] tackle this issue for natural images, but their use on computer vision tasks on medical images is unknown. Some of the assumptions made in the works [10] and [11] are unfair to the medical domain due to strict regulations, compliance rules, and the lack of availability of large, labeled datasets. Our experimentation on the two medical datasets—-COVIDx-8B [14] and COVIDx-8A [14]—-reveals that our method has better performance than FedAvg [15] in malicious environments. Our objective is to showcase a possible research direction for training a deep learning model for medical application in a secure and privacy-preserved manner. The main contributions of our article can be summarized as follows.

1) The proposed MediSecFed uses the model inversion technique to obtain the dataset for effective KD in a collaborative environment. Unlike others, we do not rely on publicly available labeled or unlabeled medical data for
KD since it is expensive to gather and annotate data in the medical domain.

2) MediSecFed shows a significant ability to learn in an environment when $20 \%$ and $40 \%$ of total participating clients are malicious clients and outperforms methods such as FedAvg by $15 \%$ on two medical datasets. Our method performs well on data gathered from multiple medical X-ray scanners and data originating from different geographical locations.

3) Our method eliminates the need to share model parameters with a single entity such as a server and secures the learned model locally. Additionally, our method is less affected by noisy malicious participants, unlike FedAvg, which does not show any signs of learning. Our method does not allow the server to perform model inversion attacks since the model parameters are never shared.

4) By allowing participants to choose desired architectures based on their compute capability and tasks, MediSecFed does not restrict the hypothesis search space. Also, MediSecFed is modular, as one can add other security and privacy features such as robust aggregation and differential privacy without significant modifications.

5) Our method exchanges logits instead of the model parameters with the server, making our method communication significantly more efficient and practical in scenarios with slower connection speeds. Unlike FedAvg, our method does not compel all the clients to have the same model after the training process, as the global model does not exist in our method. Instead, each client learns a model tailored to its specific data distribution needs.

In this section, we briefly introduced the terminologies which are closely related to our work.
A. Knowledge Distillation

KD is a compression scheme, also known as teacher–student compression, proposed by [16] that allows for the training of a smaller compact student network under the supervision of a larger pretrained teacher network or ensemble of networks, without the need for costly computation and storage. In the work [17], the authors formally introduced and generalized the term “KD,” which has since become popular among researchers. They tried to match the softmax activation function of the student’s logit with the softmax temperature activation function of the large network (teacher’s) logit. KD is widely used in knowledge transfer and model compression. However, when compared to other compression techniques, KD is capable of downsizing the network without regard for the structural difference between the teacher and student network model. Furthermore, ensemble distillation was also studied by the authors where ensemble of teacher models were considered, and where knowledge was distilled from the ensemble of network to student by doing an average of logit of the ensemble networks [18], [19]. Most of these approaches used real-world data for KD, but they could not handle cases where distillation data are not readily available. To overcome the real-world dataset dependency for KD, data-free KD was proposed in which synthetic data or metadata was used for KD [20]. DeepInversion [21] has been recently proposed in the same spirit.
B. Federated KD

The unavailability of large amounts of data, especially for the medical domain, due to data privacy concerns and legal constraints, while training a deep neural network in a distributed computation system is one of the challenging problems. FL can help to solve this problem to some extent. However, in the case of FL, model parameters are generally transferred in each communication round. Sharing a large number of parameters of deep networks incurs additional computation and communication costs. In medical domain, data collection and annotation are critical and costly tasks. Data annotation, particularly for medical images, necessitates significant effort as well as domain expertise. Federated KD [22] is thus proposed to address the aforementioned issues as well as user heterogeneity. It uses unlabeled data labeled by the teacher model (T) to transfer information from the teacher model to the small or compact student model (S). It has the potential to lessen dependency on labeled data while also ensuring privacy and security. The goal of federated KD is to reduce the L2 loss between the output logits of the teacher model (T) and the output logits of the student (S). C. Model Inversion

Recently, model inversion techniques have shown great promise for reverse-engineering the frozen model to generate the dataset on which the frozen model was trained. As mentioned in Section III-B, the features of medical images differ significantly compared to natural images, and even among the medical images, the features vary a lot. For example, the features of histopathology data are different from chest X-rays. Some of the works [10], [11] on natural images assume a public dataset is made available to clients, and KD is done using a public dataset. However, there are hardly any medical datasets of the same scale as ImageNet in the medical domain. Hence, it is not practical to assume a publicly available medical dataset for KD. Thus, our method relies on generating images from a frozen model trained on a dataset that belongs to a similar manifold. We use DeepInversion [21] to generate the images. The model inversion process starts with a random matrix of similar size as the images to be generated. DeepInversion optimizes the input while regularizing the distribution of intermediate feature maps using information stored in the batch normalization layers of the frozen model. Since batch norm layers are crucial for DeepInversion to work, it is necessary to know the architecture of the pretrained model, which we believe is a fair assumption since knowing the model architecture does not leak any privacy.
D. Model Security and Communication Efficiency

1) Model Security and Poisoning: This section details some of the security features enjoyed by our method over other algorithms like FedAvg. FedAvg enables multiple data holders to train a global model without sharing their data but by sharing their training gradients/parameters [27], [28]. Algorithms like FedAvg are not robust to attacks like poisoning via label flip poisoning or the addition of random noise. Even a single malicious client can alter the global model. Since a deep learning model can remember the training data, exchanging the model parameters with a malicious server violates the desired level of privacy. Hence, directly exchanging the model parameter/gradients is not a great idea, especially in the medical domain. On the contrary, MediSecFed significantly reduces the updates from the model parameters’ size to its output dimension. As per the work carried out in [11], a reduction in the size of the updates significantly boosts the robustness guarantee when robust aggregation algorithms are used. Furthermore, since MediSecFed does not share the model parameters with the server, the probability of model inversion attacks is close to zero. Also, unlike FedAvg, MediSecFed does not produce a single global model. Instead, each client will have the model tailored for its local dataset with some knowledge shared by the other participants via the KD process. Finally, the experimental results presented in Section IV reveal that MediSecFed is relatively robust to poisoning attacks like random noise addition. All these security and privacy features offered by our method provide a considerable advantage for a system deployed in the real world where adversaries try to hamper the overall performance of the training process.

2) Communication Efficiency: Apart from solid security features, our method is communication efficient compared to established methods like FedAvg. Consider a simple training environment with all clients with the same neural network architecture as ResNet-18. There is a total of 11 million trainable parameters in

ResNet-18. In FedAvg, the trainable parameters are exchanged in every communication round. Considering the parameters use floating-point 32 precision, the total size of weights is $4 4 ~ \mathrm { M B }$ which has to be uploaded by the client in every communication round. FedAvg is more demanding for clients with weak network connections, and the possibility of failing to upload is high because of the enormous size of the weights. It is highly likely to have an asymmetric network where upload speed is slower than download speeds in real-world applications. In MediSecFed, in every communication round, we send the logits corresponding to the number of classes in the output layer, which is very low, mostly in kilobytes (KBs). Our method improves communication efficiency by reducing the number of parameters shared from 11 million to just 10 (if the output layer of the neural network has ten classes).
We believe the above security features and communication efficiency of our method can open up industrial use cases that were not possible before with FedAvg.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS

In this section, we first provide details about the datasets used in our experiments, the details about CNN architecture and hyperparameters values are provided in Section IV-B, followed by the evaluation of the effectiveness of proposed MediSecFed in Section IV-C.
A. Datasets and Data Distribution

We evaluate the model performance on two medical datasets: modified COVIDX-8B [14] and COVIDX-8A [14]. The modified COVIDX-8B dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8B, and it consists of 5322 Chest X-Ray images of various heights and width, out of which 4922 are training images, and 400 are test images pertaining to two classes— Covid and non-Covid. The modified COVIDX-8 A dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8 A, and it has 5585 training images of various dimensions and has 400 test images pertaining to three classes—normal, pneumonia, and Covid. Both the datasets are sourced from multiple publicly available repositories, making our dataset heterogeneous. We have ensured that both datasets contain almost equal samples for all the classes by undersampling from parent datasets. Both datasets are challenging because the X-rays are captured by different devices and sourced from different geographical locations. To generate the synthetic data used for KD, we use the publicly available frozen model DenseNet-121 [29] trained on CheXpert for chest X-ray image generation.
B. Implementation Details and Hyperparameter Tuning

Our training framework relies on FedML [30], which is an open-source FL library. The total number of clients involved in the experiments is varied from five to fifteen, and all clients are available in each communication round. We use ResNet18 architecture for our homogeneous architecture experiments, and for heterogeneous client architectures, we use ResNet18 and ResNet34. We split the training dataset into train and validation sets. Validation set is used for hyperparameter tuning. We use augmentation strategies like random cropping and random rotation for X-rays (both datasets). We use the RayTune package available in the PyTorch framework to find the best set of hyperparameters. Finally, we fix the same hyperparameters, image size, architecture, and augmentation strategies for a fair comparison across all the experiments. As the designed set of experiments are computationally demanding, we crop the input to $1 2 8 \times 1 2 8$ and use Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0005. We use batch size 16 and run each experiment for at least 200 communication rounds in the case of distributed learning methods or 200 epochs in the case of local training settings. All the experiments were carried out on NVIDIA A100 GPU.

V. CONCLUSION

In this article, we have designed a new method called MediSecFed, which has leveraged the combination of techniques from KD and model inversion to perform learning in a collaborative training environment with no risk of exposing the local model or the data to a server or a third party. Furthermore, our extensive analysis of two chest $\mathbf { X }$ -ray datasets revealed the efficacy of our method, especially in a noisy environment, and outperformed FedAvg by $15 \%$ . Our method was communication efficient, and hence it can be used with slower connection speeds. We have used unbalanced non-i.i.d. data to evaluate the model’s performance, making our method suitable for any real-world industrial application.

In the future, we would like to extend our work to further improve the accuracy of our method by enhancing the diversity of the generated data used for KD. Also, we would like to explore the use of our method on other medical datasets.

MediSecFed: Private and Secure Medical Image Classification in the Presence of Malicious Clients

Abhinav Kumar $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Vishal Purohit $\textcircled{1}$ , Vandana Bharti $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Rishav Singh, Member, IEEE, and Sanjay Kumar Singh $\textcircled{1}$ , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—Deep learning demonstrates its efficacy and potential to solve challenging computer vision problems in medical and other industrial applications. Federated learning is a learning paradigm that facilitates collaborative learning in a federation of users without exchanging actual data with a single authority like a server. However, federated learning provides only a basic level of privacy and robustness and is vulnerable to model poisoning and model inversion attacks in hostile training environments. Hence, in this article, we propose MediSecFed—a secure framework for federated learning in a hostile environment. Compared to the widely used FedAvg, our method relies on simple and practical ideas from knowledge distillation and model inversion to ensure additional security and privacy features. Our approach achieves knowledge exchange among participating entities without sharing model parameters as FedAvg does, thus protecting the privacy of the local data from the server and significantly reducing communication costs. We evaluate our method on two chest $\pmb { \mathrm { x } }$ -ray datasets. Our method outperforms FedAvg by $15 \%$ on both datasets in a hostile environment. Our method will also continue to maintain good performance even if the number of malicious participating entities increases. Robustness to learn in a malicious environment while preserving privacy with reduced communication costs makes our method more desirable and efficient than that of FedAvg.
Index Terms—COVID-19, data-free knowledge distillation, federated learning (FL), medical data security, privacypreserving.
I. INTRODUCTION

W ITH the unprecedented growth of computer softwareand hardware technologies, an increasing amount of medical data from medical institutions, patients, health insurers, and pharma industries are becoming readily accessible. This access affords enormous scope for data science technologies to extract data-driven insights and improve the quality of medical predictions. The deep learning industry has seen significant growth in the last several years, and it has tremendous scope in building useful and high potential IoT-based applications. With AlexNet’s breakthrough in the ImageNet competition in 2012, more advanced deep neural networks (ResNet, VGGNet, and several others) have been developed. Deep learning is now widely used in industrial applications by utilizing vast amounts of generated datasets. Recently, the deep learning model has shown its potential in healthcare applications as a feature extractor for cancer prediction [1].

However, to produce good results, these networks require a huge amount of computation and a vast number of datasets. As a result, the full potential of these networks can only be realized through extensive computational programming with large datasets. In the distributed setting of healthcare applications, medical data are typically fragmented and private, making it difficult to create robust results among communities. Different medical institutions may be able to access only the clinical records of their respective patient communities. However, these records are susceptible since they contain patients’ private health information. Strict regulations and government laws have been devised to manage the process of obtaining and analyzing such data. This presents a major hurdle for creating successful, generalized, deep learning-based models that require varied and large amounts of medical data. Data sharing among medical institutions is becoming increasingly desirable to minimize the shortage and distribution biases of medical data and enhance model performance on critical tasks.

Moreover, sharing medical data with a third party is a major concern to the data owner or institution, even if the third party is well known or anonymous. Besides that, due to the potential conflict of interest in each medical institution, it is also impractical to aggregate sensitive data from IoT devices in different hospitals to build an efficient model for healthcare diagnostic systems.

It enables training a shared global model using a central server while retaining all sensitive data in the local medical institution where it belongs. FL has tremendous potential for connecting fragmented healthcare data sources while maintaining privacy. It enables learning from distributed data sources by aggregating the locally obtained model parameters without transmitting sensitive health data. However, there are major impediments to the scalable deployment of secure and truly privacy-preserving FL for sensitive applications. Existing FL algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial updates [3] and backdoor attacks [4], and they can expose sensitive information on local datasets [5]. This jeopardizes personal privacy and has the potential to result in unforeseen economic and life losses. In some ways, the privacy issues in FL constitute a significant impediment to the marketing and development of industrial artificial intelligence based applications.

The key challenges in federated training are communication overheads and client heterogeneity: Training data, as well as hardware and computing resources, can vary dramatically between clients, e.g., when training on mobile devices. The primary goal of the medical data classification problem is to train a model that can produce good results on the test datasets. To accomplish this, we train a huge model, which could be an ensemble of several individual trained models or just a very large model trained using a regularizer such as a Dropout. Once the huge model (teacher) is trained, we utilize a process known as distillation to transfer the complicated knowledge gained by the huge model to a smaller model (student) that is more suited for deployment in devices with limited memory and compute power. The huge model must generalize properly so that when we are distilling knowledge to the smaller model, it can generalize in the same way as the large model. Hence, knowledge distillation (KD) [6], a new technique for compacting and accelerating neural networks, is developed to maintain comparable performance while keeping the constraints in mind.

Despite the favorable outcomes, KD techniques rely heavily on huge amounts of training data to transmit information from pretrained teacher models to students. However, owing to privacy or transmission concerns, the training data are sometimes not shared alongside the pretrained models, rendering these approaches inapplicable. Another limitation is KD’s reliance on proxy data, as the selection of proxy data, which requires careful consideration, is a critical factor in distillation performance. To solve this issue, data-free KD is proposed [7]. Data-free KD generally uses the generated surrogate data based on the large network (teacher) for training a fast and compact (student) network. Some researchers [7] prefer to generate surrogate data by using the statistical metadata of the activation in a large network (teacher).

While model inversion (MI) [8] is another strategy for generating synthesized data for training student networks, it is a critical step in the data-free KD process, with the objective of recovering training data from pretrained teacher models. Student models may be easily learned using the generated synthetic data by directly using the data-driven KD methods. Recently, a generative adversarial network has demonstrated its potential in image synthesis and translation, becoming a popular choice for such applications [9]. In general, sensitive and confidential data in the healthcare domain necessitates security in a distributed environment. In order to be processed through deep learning based approaches, data must be centralized, but owing to medical data privacy regulations, collecting and sharing patients’ data in a centralized data server is often not feasible. Also, in the case of a new disease such as COVID-19, there is a lack of vast amounts of annotated training data at a single site. Therefore, in this study, we have attempted to tackle the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms.

Motivation and Contribution: FL ensures a basic level of privacy by not exchanging the actual data with any other participating entity. Yet it trades the model’s parameters with a server. To subvert the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL algorithms, we propose a method called MediSecFed. Our approach takes inspiration from KD and model inversion literature to build a framework that ensures good performance without trading off client privacy. Inherently, our method reduces the communication cost significantly while preserving privacy. To the best of our knowledge, most of the works [10]–[13] tackle this issue for natural images, but their use on computer vision tasks on medical images is unknown. Some of the assumptions made in the works [10] and [11] are unfair to the medical domain due to strict regulations, compliance rules, and the lack of availability of large, labeled datasets. Our experimentation on the two medical datasets—-COVIDx-8B [14] and COVIDx-8A [14]—-reveals that our method has better performance than FedAvg [15] in malicious environments. Our objective is to showcase a possible research direction for training a deep learning model for medical application in a secure and privacy-preserved manner. The main contributions of our article can be summarized as follows.

1) The proposed MediSecFed uses the model inversion technique to obtain the dataset for effective KD in a collaborative environment. Unlike others, we do not rely on publicly available labeled or unlabeled medical data for
KD since it is expensive to gather and annotate data in the medical domain.

2) MediSecFed shows a significant ability to learn in an environment when $20 \%$ and $40 \%$ of total participating clients are malicious clients and outperforms methods such as FedAvg by $15 \%$ on two medical datasets. Our method performs well on data gathered from multiple medical X-ray scanners and data originating from different geographical locations.

3) Our method eliminates the need to share model parameters with a single entity such as a server and secures the learned model locally. Additionally, our method is less affected by noisy malicious participants, unlike FedAvg, which does not show any signs of learning. Our method does not allow the server to perform model inversion attacks since the model parameters are never shared.

4) By allowing participants to choose desired architectures based on their compute capability and tasks, MediSecFed does not restrict the hypothesis search space. Also, MediSecFed is modular, as one can add other security and privacy features such as robust aggregation and differential privacy without significant modifications.

5) Our method exchanges logits instead of the model parameters with the server, making our method communication significantly more efficient and practical in scenarios with slower connection speeds. Unlike FedAvg, our method does not compel all the clients to have the same model after the training process, as the global model does not exist in our method. Instead, each client learns a model tailored to its specific data distribution needs.

II. PRELIMINARIES
In this section, we briefly introduced the terminologies which are closely related to our work.
A. Knowledge Distillation

KD is a compression scheme, also known as teacher–student compression, proposed by [16] that allows for the training of a smaller compact student network under the supervision of a larger pretrained teacher network or ensemble of networks, without the need for costly computation and storage. In the work [17], the authors formally introduced and generalized the term “KD,” which has since become popular among researchers. They tried to match the softmax activation function of the student’s logit with the softmax temperature activation function of the large network (teacher’s) logit. KD is widely used in knowledge transfer and model compression. However, when compared to other compression techniques, KD is capable of downsizing the network without regard for the structural difference between the teacher and student network model. Furthermore, ensemble distillation was also studied by the authors where ensemble of teacher models were considered, and where knowledge was distilled from the ensemble of network to student by doing an average of logit of the ensemble networks [18], [19]. Most of these approaches used real-world data for KD, but they could not handle cases where distillation data are not readily available. To overcome the real-world dataset dependency for KD, data-free KD was proposed in which synthetic data or metadata was used for KD [20]. DeepInversion [21] has been recently proposed in the same spirit.
B. Federated KD

The unavailability of large amounts of data, especially for the medical domain, due to data privacy concerns and legal constraints, while training a deep neural network in a distributed computation system is one of the challenging problems. FL can help to solve this problem to some extent. However, in the case of FL, model parameters are generally transferred in each communication round. Sharing a large number of parameters of deep networks incurs additional computation and communication costs. In medical domain, data collection and annotation are critical and costly tasks. Data annotation, particularly for medical images, necessitates significant effort as well as domain expertise. Federated KD [22] is thus proposed to address the aforementioned issues as well as user heterogeneity. It uses unlabeled data labeled by the teacher model (T) to transfer information from the teacher model to the small or compact student model (S). It has the potential to lessen dependency on labeled data while also ensuring privacy and security. The goal of federated KD is to reduce the L2 loss between the output logits of the teacher model (T) and the output logits of the student (S). C. Model Inversion

Recently, model inversion techniques have shown great promise for reverse-engineering the frozen model to generate the dataset on which the frozen model was trained. As mentioned in Section III-B, the features of medical images differ significantly compared to natural images, and even among the medical images, the features vary a lot. For example, the features of histopathology data are different from chest X-rays. Some of the works [10], [11] on natural images assume a public dataset is made available to clients, and KD is done using a public dataset. However, there are hardly any medical datasets of the same scale as ImageNet in the medical domain. Hence, it is not practical to assume a publicly available medical dataset for KD. Thus, our method relies on generating images from a frozen model trained on a dataset that belongs to a similar manifold. We use DeepInversion [21] to generate the images. The model inversion process starts with a random matrix of similar size as the images to be generated. DeepInversion optimizes the input while regularizing the distribution of intermediate feature maps using information stored in the batch normalization layers of the frozen model. Since batch norm layers are crucial for DeepInversion to work, it is necessary to know the architecture of the pretrained model, which we believe is a fair assumption since knowing the model architecture does not leak any privacy.
D. Model Security and Communication Efficiency

1) Model Security and Poisoning: This section details some of the security features enjoyed by our method over other algorithms like FedAvg. FedAvg enables multiple data holders to train a global model without sharing their data but by sharing their training gradients/parameters [27], [28]. Algorithms like FedAvg are not robust to attacks like poisoning via label flip poisoning or the addition of random noise. Even a single malicious client can alter the global model. Since a deep learning model can remember the training data, exchanging the model parameters with a malicious server violates the desired level of privacy. Hence, directly exchanging the model parameter/gradients is not a great idea, especially in the medical domain. On the contrary, MediSecFed significantly reduces the updates from the model parameters’ size to its output dimension. As per the work carried out in [11], a reduction in the size of the updates significantly boosts the robustness guarantee when robust aggregation algorithms are used. Furthermore, since MediSecFed does not share the model parameters with the server, the probability of model inversion attacks is close to zero. Also, unlike FedAvg, MediSecFed does not produce a single global model. Instead, each client will have the model tailored for its local dataset with some knowledge shared by the other participants via the KD process. Finally, the experimental results presented in Section IV reveal that MediSecFed is relatively robust to poisoning attacks like random noise addition. All these security and privacy features offered by our method provide a considerable advantage for a system deployed in the real world where adversaries try to hamper the overall performance of the training process.

2) Communication Efficiency: Apart from solid security features, our method is communication efficient compared to established methods like FedAvg. Consider a simple training environment with all clients with the same neural network architecture as ResNet-18. There is a total of 11 million trainable parameters in

ResNet-18. In FedAvg, the trainable parameters are exchanged in every communication round. Considering the parameters use floating-point 32 precision, the total size of weights is $4 4 ~ \mathrm { M B }$ which has to be uploaded by the client in every communication round. FedAvg is more demanding for clients with weak network connections, and the possibility of failing to upload is high because of the enormous size of the weights. It is highly likely to have an asymmetric network where upload speed is slower than download speeds in real-world applications. In MediSecFed, in every communication round, we send the logits corresponding to the number of classes in the output layer, which is very low, mostly in kilobytes (KBs). Our method improves communication efficiency by reducing the number of parameters shared from 11 million to just 10 (if the output layer of the neural network has ten classes).
We believe the above security features and communication efficiency of our method can open up industrial use cases that were not possible before with FedAvg.

A. Datasets and Data Distribution

We evaluate the model performance on two medical datasets: modified COVIDX-8B [14] and COVIDX-8A [14]. The modified COVIDX-8B dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8B, and it consists of 5322 Chest X-Ray images of various heights and width, out of which 4922 are training images, and 400 are test images pertaining to two classes— Covid and non-Covid. The modified COVIDX-8 A dataset is undersampled from the original dataset COVIDx-8 A, and it has 5585 training images of various dimensions and has 400 test images pertaining to three classes—normal, pneumonia, and Covid. Both the datasets are sourced from multiple publicly available repositories, making our dataset heterogeneous. We have ensured that both datasets contain almost equal samples for all the classes by undersampling from parent datasets. Both datasets are challenging because the X-rays are captured by different devices and sourced from different geographical locations. To generate the synthetic data used for KD, we use the publicly available frozen model DenseNet-121 [29] trained on CheXpert for chest X-ray image generation.
B. Implementation Details and Hyperparameter Tuning

Our training framework relies on FedML [30], which is an open-source FL library. The total number of clients involved in the experiments is varied from five to fifteen, and all clients are available in each communication round. We use ResNet18 architecture for our homogeneous architecture experiments, and for heterogeneous client architectures, we use ResNet18 and ResNet34. We split the training dataset into train and validation sets. Validation set is used for hyperparameter tuning. We use augmentation strategies like random cropping and random rotation for X-rays (both datasets). We use the RayTune package available in the PyTorch framework to find the best set of hyperparameters. Finally, we fix the same hyperparameters, image size, architecture, and augmentation strategies for a fair comparison across all the experiments. As the designed set of experiments are computationally demanding, we crop the input to $1 2 8 \times 1 2 8$ and use Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0005. We use batch size 16 and run each experiment for at least 200 communication rounds in the case of distributed learning methods or 200 epochs in the case of local training settings. All the experiments were carried out on NVIDIA A100 GPU.

V. CONCLUSION

In this article, we have designed a new method called MediSecFed, which has leveraged the combination of techniques from KD and model inversion to perform learning in a collaborative training environment with no risk of exposing the local model or the data to a server or a third party. Furthermore, our extensive analysis of two chest $\mathbf { X }$ -ray datasets revealed the efficacy of our method, especially in a noisy environment, and outperformed FedAvg by $15 \%$ . Our method was communication efficient, and hence it can be used with slower connection speeds. We have used unbalanced non-i.i.d. data to evaluate the model’s performance, making our method suitable for any real-world industrial application.

In the future, we would like to extend our work to further improve the accuracy of our method by enhancing the diversity of the generated data used for KD. Also, we would like to explore the use of our method on other medical datasets.

MediSecFed: Private and Secure Medical Image Classification in the Presence of Malicious Clients

Abhinav Kumar $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Vishal Purohit $\textcircled{1}$ , Vandana Bharti $\textcircled{1}$ , Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Rishav Singh, Member, IEEE, and Sanjay Kumar Singh $\textcircled{1}$ , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—Deep learning demonstrates its efficacy and potential to solve challenging computer vision problems in medical and other industrial applications. Federated learning is a learning paradigm that facilitates collaborative learning in a federation of users without exchanging actual data with a single authority like a server. However, federated learning provides only a basic level of privacy and robustness and is vulnerable to model poisoning and model inversion attacks in hostile training environments. Hence, in this article, we propose MediSecFed—a secure framework for federated learning in a hostile environment. Compared to the widely used FedAvg, our method relies on simple and practical ideas from knowledge distillation and model inversion to ensure additional security and privacy features. Our approach achieves knowledge exchange among participating entities without sharing model parameters as FedAvg does, thus protecting the privacy of the local data from the server and significantly reducing communication costs. We evaluate our method on two chest $\pmb { \chi }$ -ray datasets. Our method outperforms FedAvg by $15 \%$ on both datasets in a hostile environment. Our method will also continue to maintain good performance even if the number of malicious participating entities increases. Robustness to learn in a malicious environment while preserving privacy with reduced communication costs makes our method more desirable and efficient than that of FedAvg.
Index Terms—COVID-19, data-free knowledge distillation, federated learning (FL), medical data security, privacypreserving.
I. INTRODUCTION

W ITH the unprecedented growth of computer softwareand hardware technologies, an increasing amount of medical data from medical institutions, patients, health insurers, and pharma industries are becoming readily accessible. This access affords enormous scope for data science technologies to extract data-driven insights and improve the quality of medical predictions. The deep learning industry has seen significant growth in the last several years, and it has tremendous scope in building useful and high potential IoT-based applications. With AlexNet’s breakthrough in the ImageNet competition in 2012, more advanced deep neural networks (ResNet, VGGNet, and several others) have been developed. Deep learning is now widely used in industrial applications by utilizing vast amounts of generated datasets. Recently, the deep learning model has shown its potential in healthcare applications as a feature extractor for cancer prediction [1].

However, to produce good results, these networks require a huge amount of computation and a vast number of datasets. As a result, the full potential of these networks can only be realized through extensive computational programming with large datasets. In the distributed setting of healthcare applications, medical data are typically fragmented and private, making it difficult to create robust results among communities. Different medical institutions may be able to access only the clinical records of their respective patient communities. However, these records are susceptible since they contain patients’ private health information. Strict regulations and government laws have been devised to manage the process of obtaining and analyzing such data. This presents a major hurdle for creating successful, generalized, deep learning-based models that require varied and large amounts of medical data. Data sharing among medical institutions is becoming increasingly desirable to minimize the shortage and distribution biases of medical data and enhance model performance on critical tasks.

Moreover, sharing medical data with a third party is a major concern to the data owner or institution, even if the third party is well known or anonymous. Besides that, due to the potential conflict of interest in each medical institution, it is also impractical to aggregate sensitive data from IoT devices in different hospitals to build an efficient model for healthcare diagnostic systems.
